results.title: Data subject asks for their data
results.answer:
This is a data subject access request under **s23 of POPIA**. Once you've verified who they are, the customer is entitled to:

- **confirmation, free of charge,** of whether you hold personal information about them (s23(1)(a));
- **the record or a description of it**, including the **identity of all third parties, or categories of third parties, that have had access to it** (s23(1)(b)).

Under s25, the procedure follows PAIA. Here's how to handle it.

## 1. Check you're the responsible party (day 0)

- **If the data belongs to your client and you're only the operator** (for example, you host or run a system for another business), don't answer it yourself. Forward the request to the client promptly and tell the customer you've done so.
- **If you're the responsible party**, carry on below.

## 2. Log it and acknowledge it (day 0–2)

Open a request record with:
- date received and channel;
- the requester's details;
- what was asked for;
- the due date: **30 days**. That's the PAIA timeline for private bodies. You can extend it once by up to 30 days, but only with written notice and reasons before the first deadline.
- who's handling it.

Acknowledge receipt quickly (draft below). If there's a dispute or legal threat in the background, take advice before you release anything. Access requests are sometimes used as pre-litigation discovery, and privileged material can be withheld.

## 3. Verify identity proportionately

Don't hand someone's data to an impersonator. Don't over-collect to check, either.

- **Reply to the email address you already have on file**, not to a new address that only appears in the request.
- **Match two things you already hold**, for example an account or order number plus the mobile number on file, or the last invoice amount.
- **Logged-in users:** re-authenticating in the app is enough.
- **Don't ask for an ID copy** unless you already hold their ID number and can't verify any other way. Never ask for more personal information than you already hold.

## 4. Find everything

Use your ROPA or data map (`templates/ropa.csv`) as the checklist, and search every place their information could be:

| Where | Examples |
|---|---|
| Product database | profile, orders, bookings, support tickets, consent records, audit logs about them |
| CRM / helpdesk | Salesforce, HubSpot, Zendesk, Freshdesk notes and call logs |
| Email and chat | shared inboxes, staff mailboxes, WhatsApp Business, Slack mentions |
| Finance | invoices, payment records (show masked card or account numbers only) |
| Marketing | Mailchimp/Brevo lists, consent and opt-out history, ad audiences you uploaded them to |
| Analytics and logs | records linked to their user ID or email |
| Spreadsheets and drives | exports, lead lists, shared Google Sheets |
| Operators | anything your vendors hold for you that you can retrieve |
| Backups | You don't need to restore backups. State that copies exist in backups and when they expire. |

## 5. Review before release

- **Third parties:** redact other people's personal information, such as other customers and staff personal details. PAIA lets you sever the parts you may refuse and release the rest.
- **Lawful refusals:** you may refuse parts only on the PAIA grounds for private bodies (s23(4)(a)). The main ones are another person's privacy, confidential commercial information of a third party, and legal privilege. Record the ground for each item withheld. Refusing on "it's a lot of work" is not a ground.
- **Accuracy:** if you spot information that's wrong, note it. They may follow up with a correction or deletion request under s24 (Form 2, free).

## 6. Respond

Include:
1. confirmation that you hold their information;
2. a copy of it, in a commonly used readable format (PDF, or CSV/JSON for data);
3. a description of each category: what it is, why you hold it, where it came from, and how long you keep it;
4. **who has had access**: named operators and third parties (hosting, CRM, email platform, payment provider, couriers and so on), and whether any of it is processed outside SA;
5. anything withheld and the ground;
6. their next options: correction or deletion (s24, Form 2), objection (s11(3), Form 1), and the right to complain to the Information Regulator.

**Fees.** Confirming whether you hold data is always free. PAIA doesn't charge a personal requester the request fee for their own records. A reproduction fee may be allowed, but if you charge anything you must give a written estimate first (s23(2)). For one customer, it's usually not worth charging.

**Delivery.** Use a password-protected file with the password sent by SMS, or an expiring download link. Don't attach a large unprotected export to a plain email.

Close the log entry with the date sent, what was sent and anything withheld. Keep the log; it's your evidence (s8, s11(2)(a)).

---

## Draft 1: acknowledgement and verification

> **Subject:** Your request for your personal information, ref DSAR-2026-0xx
>
> Dear [Name]
>
> Thank you for your request of [date] for the personal information [Registered name] (Pty) Ltd, trading as [Trading name], holds about you. We're handling it under section 23 of the Protection of Personal Information Act.
>
> To protect your information, we need to confirm it's you before we release anything. Please reply from this email address with [your account/order number] and [the mobile number on your account].
>
> Once we've verified your identity, we'll respond within 30 days, by [due date]. There's no charge for this request.
>
> Kind regards
> [Name], Information Officer
> [Registered name] (Pty) Ltd · [address] · privacy@[domain].co.za

## Draft 2: response

> **Subject:** Your personal information, ref DSAR-2026-0xx
>
> Dear [Name]
>
> We confirm that we hold personal information about you. A copy is attached as a password-protected file; we've sent the password to your mobile number ending in [xx].
>
> **What we hold and why**
> - Account details (name, email, mobile): to provide your account. Kept until [period] after you close your account.
> - Orders and invoices: to fulfil orders and meet tax obligations. Kept for [5 years, confirm with your accountant].
> - Support conversations: to help you. Kept for [period].
> - Marketing preferences: your consent and opt-out history, kept for as long as we market to anyone so we can honour your choice.
>
> *(Replace the bracketed periods with your actual retention schedule.)*
>
> **Who has had access**
> [Hosting provider], [CRM], [email platform], [payment provider], [courier]. These service providers process your information on our behalf under written agreements. [Hosting provider / email platform] store data outside South Africa, under agreements that require protection equivalent to POPIA.
>
> [**Information not included:** We've removed other people's personal details from [records], as the law requires.]
>
> **Your options**
> - Ask us to correct or delete information (section 24).
> - Object to some processing (section 11(3)).
> - Withdraw marketing consent at any time.
> - Complain to the Information Regulator: www.inforegulator.org.za, complaints.IR@inforegulator.org.za.
>
> Kind regards
> [Name], Information Officer

---

**For next time:** if these requests become regular, build a "Download my data" export into the product and keep a written runbook with an SLA. `scripts/popia_pack.py` can draft one, and there's a DSAR runbook in `templates/`. Also check that your privacy notice and PAIA manual tell people how to make these requests.

*This is engineering and compliance guidance, not legal advice.* If you're thinking of withholding anything, or the customer is in a dispute with you, have a POPIA attorney review the response before you send it.

results.title: Objection to processing
results.answer:
**Almost certainly yes, for the profiling.** For "customer insights" profiling, the lawful basis is nearly always legitimate interests, and once someone has objected to processing on that basis you have to stop it. You don't usually have to stop serving them as a customer.

## Why

It depends on the **lawful basis** you're relying on for the profiling under s11(1):

| Your basis for the profiling | Effect of the objection |
|---|---|
| **Legitimate interests** of you or a third party, s11(1)(f). This is the usual one for analytics and segmentation | The data subject may object **on reasonable grounds** (s11(3)(a)). Once they've objected, you **may no longer process** their PI for that purpose (s11(4)). |
| Their own legitimate interest (s11(1)(d)), or a public law duty (s11(1)(e)) | Same as above. |
| **Consent** (s11(1)(a)) | Treat it as a **withdrawal of consent** (s11(2)(b)). Stop from now on. What you did before the withdrawal stays lawful. |
| The profiling feeds **direct marketing** (segments, targeting, personalised offers) | They can object to that **at any time**, and they don't have to give reasons (s11(3)(b)). Stop. |
| Contract (s11(1)(b)) or legal obligation (s11(1)(c)) | The s11(3) objection right doesn't attach to these bases. But "customer insights" profiling is very rarely *necessary* to perform a contract or comply with a law. Don't relabel the basis after the fact to get around the objection. |

POPIA is stricter than the GDPR here. The GDPR lets a controller carry on if it shows "compelling legitimate grounds". POPIA has no such override: under s11(4) you **may no longer process**. The only argument open to you is that the objection wasn't made "on reasonable grounds". That's a weak position for discretionary analytics, and it's a poor fight to pick when the person can complain to the Information Regulator (s74). **Practical answer: stop.**

## What to do now

1. **Log the objection.** Record the date received, the channel, what they objected to, and their identity check. You don't need to make them use **Form 1**. Reg 2 (as amended in 2025) makes objections free of charge and lets people submit them through several channels, so accept an email, a chat message or a support ticket.
2. **Identify the processing it covers.** Look at what feeds the profile: behavioural events, purchase history, enrichment data, segmentation models, any "propensity" or "churn" scores.
3. **Stop the processing for this person**, everywhere it happens:
   - Add a suppression flag (e.g. `profiling_objected = true`) that your pipelines check **at processing time**, not only when a batch is built.
   - Exclude them from segments, lookalike audiences and model scoring.
   - Tell your **operators** (analytics, CDP or CRM vendors, ad platforms) to stop too. Under s20/s21 they act on your instructions.
4. **Deal with what you've already derived.** Their existing profile, scores and segment memberships have no remaining purpose, so delete or de-identify them (s14(4)). Keep the **record of the objection itself** and the suppression flag. You need those to prove compliance and to stop them being profiled again.
5. **Keep the rest of the relationship going.** Orders, billing, support and legally required records continue under contract or legal obligation. The objection is about the profiling, not the whole account.
6. **Check for automated decisions.** If the insights drive decisions with legal or substantial effects (pricing, eligibility, credit limits, fraud blocks), s71 also applies. Make sure no such decision about this person rests solely on the profile.
7. **Reply in writing within a reasonable time.** Aim for about 30 days or less. Confirm what you've stopped, what you'll keep and why, and that they can complain to the Information Regulator.

## Reply you can adapt

> Subject: Your objection to customer insights processing
>
> Dear [Name],
>
> Thank you for your message of [date]. We have recorded your objection under section 11(3) of the Protection of Personal Information Act.
>
> With effect from [date], we have stopped using your personal information for customer insights and profiling. You have been excluded from our analytics segments and models. We have also asked our service providers who help with this processing to do the same. The profile information we had built about you has been [deleted / de-identified].
>
> We will continue to process the information we need to [provide your account / fulfil orders / meet our legal record-keeping duties]. This processing is based on our contract with you or on legal obligations, not on the processing you objected to. We keep a record of your objection so that we don't profile you again.
>
> If you are not satisfied with how we have handled your objection, you can contact our Information Officer at [email] or lodge a complaint with the Information Regulator (www.inforegulator.org.za, POPIAComplaints@inforegulator.org.za).
>
> Kind regards,
> [Name], Information Officer, [Responsible party]

results.answer:
Here's a POPIA-aligned privacy notice for your salon booking app. It covers everything s18 says you must tell people when you collect their information. It also covers your three operators (Supabase, Resend and Google Analytics) and the cross-border transfers they create under s72.

Fill in the `[square brackets]`. Then work through the **"Before you publish"** checklist at the end. Some statements in the notice are only true once you've made the matching change in the app, especially the Google Analytics consent.

Save it as `privacy.md`, or as a `/privacy` route in your Lovable app. Link to it from the booking form, the sign-up screen and the site footer.

---

# Privacy Notice

**[Salon trading name]**, operated by **[Registered legal name, e.g. ABC Hair (Pty) Ltd / sole proprietor's full name]**
Last updated: [date] · Version [1.0]

## 1. Who we are

We are [Salon trading name], a hair salon at [street address, Pretoria]. Under the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 ("POPIA"), we are the **responsible party** for the personal information you give us when you book through [app/website URL].

**Information Officer:** [Name], [email], [phone]
Postal / physical address: [address]

## 2. What we collect and why

| Information | When we collect it | Why we need it | Required? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Name, mobile number, email address | When you book or create an account | To make, confirm and manage your booking, and to contact you about it | **Required.** We can't take a booking without it |
| Booking details (service, stylist, date, time, booking history) | When you book | To deliver the service, manage our diary and keep your booking history | Required |
| Login details (email, encrypted password) | If you create an account | To let you sign in and manage your bookings | Only if you choose to have an account |
| Booking notes you type in | Optional | To prepare for your appointment | Optional. Please don't share medical information here (see section 4) |
| Device and usage information (pages visited, approximate location from IP, browser type, cookie identifiers) | When you use the app, **only if you accept analytics cookies** | To understand how the app is used and to improve it | Optional. Declining has no effect on booking |
| Payment confirmation [if applicable] | When you pay a deposit | To record payment | Required for paid bookings. We do not store card numbers; [payment provider] handles them |

We collect this information **directly from you**. We collect only what we need for these purposes (s10). If you don't provide the required information, we can't accept or confirm your booking.

## 3. Our legal grounds (s11 of POPIA)

- **Contract (s11(1)(b)):** processing your booking and account information so we can provide the service you asked for.
- **Legal obligation (s11(1)(c)):** keeping financial records as tax law requires.
- **Legitimate interests (s11(1)(f)):** securing the app, preventing no-shows and fraud, and handling disputes.
- **Consent (s11(1)(a)):** analytics cookies and any marketing messages. You can withdraw consent at any time.

## 4. Sensitive information

We do not ask for **special personal information**, such as health information. If you tell us about something like an allergy or a scalp condition so we can do your treatment safely, we use it only for that appointment and with your consent (s27(1)(a)). Please tell your stylist in person rather than writing it in the booking notes.

## 5. Children

Our app is meant for adults (18+). If you book for a child, you confirm that you are their parent or legal guardian. Please give only the child's first name and the service they need (s35(1)(a)).

## 6. Messages we send

- **Service messages:** booking confirmations, reminders, changes and cancellations. You'll get these because they're part of the service.
- **Marketing (specials, promotions, newsletters):** we send these **only if you tick the opt-in box**. We may also send them if you're an existing client and the offer is for similar services from us; you can refuse when you book and in every message (s69). Every marketing message tells you who it's from and has a free, simple way to unsubscribe.

## 7. Who we share information with

We do **not** sell your personal information. We share it only with service providers ("operators") who process it on our behalf. They work under written agreements that require them to keep it confidential and secure (s20 and s21).

| Operator | What they do | Where the data is held |
|---|---|---|
| **Supabase** | Database, user accounts and app backend | European Union ([region, e.g. Frankfurt, Germany]) |
| **Resend** | Sending booking confirmations and reminder emails | [United States / EU, depending on the sending region you set] |
| **Google Analytics (Google LLC / Google Ireland)** | Website and app usage statistics (only if you accept analytics cookies) | United States and other countries where Google operates |
| **Lovable** / [hosting provider] | Hosting the app's front end | [Country] |
| [Payment provider, e.g. Yoco / PayFast / Paystack] | Processing deposits [if applicable] | [Country] |

We may also disclose information when the law requires it, or to protect our legal rights.

## 8. Information sent outside South Africa (s72)

Our service providers store or process your information **outside South Africa**: in the European Union (Supabase) and in the United States (Resend and Google). We send it only:

- where the recipient is bound by law or by a binding agreement giving a level of protection substantially similar to POPIA. The EU's GDPR applies to our Supabase data, and our providers' data processing agreements cover the rest; or
- where the transfer is necessary to provide the booking service you asked for (s72(1)(c)); or
- for analytics, where you've consented (s72(1)(b)).

## 9. Cookies

- **Strictly necessary cookies** (log-in session, security) are always on. The app doesn't work without them.
- **Analytics cookies** (Google Analytics) load **only after you click "Accept"** on our cookie banner. You can change your choice at any time via [Cookie settings link]. We have set Google Analytics to [anonymise IP addresses / not use advertising features].

We don't use advertising or tracking pixels. [Delete this sentence if you add Meta, TikTok or Google Ads pixels.]

## 10. How long we keep information (s14)

| Information | How long |
|---|---|
| Booking history and contact details | [24 months] after your last booking, then deleted or de-identified |
| Account | Until you delete it, or after [24 months] of inactivity |
| Invoices / payment records | 5 years, as tax law requires |
| Analytics data | [14 months] (Google Analytics retention setting) |
| Marketing consent and opt-out records | For as long as we market to you, plus [2 years] as proof |

Backups are overwritten within [7 / 30] days of deletion.

## 11. How we protect your information (s19)

- All connections are encrypted (HTTPS).
- Data is encrypted at rest.
- Database access is restricted so you can see only your own bookings.
- Staff access is limited and protected by multi-factor authentication.

If we have reasonable grounds to believe your information has been accessed by an unauthorised person, we will notify you and the Information Regulator as soon as reasonably possible (s22).

## 12. Your rights

You have the right to:

- **ask whether we hold your information and get a copy of it**, free of charge (s23);
- **ask us to correct or delete** information that is inaccurate, out of date, excessive or unlawfully obtained (s24, Form 2);
- **object** to processing based on our legitimate interests, and to direct marketing at any time (s11(3), Form 1);
- **withdraw consent** at any time (s11(2)(b)). This doesn't affect processing done before you withdrew;
- **unsubscribe** from marketing using the link in any message;
- **complain to the Information Regulator** (see below).

To use any of these rights, email [privacy@salon.co.za], or use [Account → Delete my account / Download my data] in the app. We'll check who you are using details we already hold. We'll respond within [30] days. You don't need a special form, but we will also accept the prescribed Forms 1 and 2.

**Information Regulator (South Africa)**
Website: www.inforegulator.org.za
Complaints: POPIAComplaints@inforegulator.org.za
[Check the Regulator's current physical address on its website before publishing.]

## 13. Access to information (PAIA)

Our PAIA manual is available at [link] or on request from our Information Officer.

## 14. Changes to this notice

We'll update this notice when our practices change. The date at the top always shows the latest version. If we make important changes, we'll notify you by email or in the app.

---

## Before you publish: make the notice true

1. **Google Analytics consent (High if missing).** The notice says GA loads only after the user accepts. Lovable apps typically paste the GA tag straight into `index.html`, which means it loads before any choice is made. To fix it:
   - Add a cookie banner with equally prominent **Accept** and **Reject** buttons. The consent banner in `registry/` drops into a Lovable/Vite app.
   - Set Consent Mode defaults to `denied` before the tag loads:
     `gtag('consent','default',{ad_storage:'denied',ad_user_data:'denied',ad_personalization:'denied',analytics_storage:'denied'})`
   - Load GA only after the user accepts.
   - Turn off Google Signals and advertising features. Set data retention to the shortest period that works for you.
2. **Marketing opt-in.** Add a separate, unticked checkbox on the booking form, and store a consent record (who, the exact wording, when). Keep reminders and marketing apart in Resend.
3. **Resend region.** Check which sending region you configured: US is the default; EU regions are available. Update section 7 to match.
4. **Supabase RLS.** Turn on row-level security for every table (bookings, profiles), with policies scoped to the owner. Make sure the service-role key never appears in the Lovable front end; only the anon key should be there. Section 11 claims this is in place.
5. **Data processing agreements.** Accept or download the DPAs from Supabase, Resend and Google. These are your s21 written contracts and your s72(1)(a) "binding agreement". Record them in a ROPA (`templates/ropa.csv`).
6. **Rights path.** Make sure the privacy email exists and someone monitors it. Ideally add "Delete my account" and "Download my data" to the app.
7. **Retention job.** Schedule a deletion job (e.g. Supabase `pg_cron`) that enforces the periods in section 10. Without one, the retention table is a promise you're breaking.
8. **Information Officer.** Register the IO on the Regulator's **eServices portal** (s55(2)). By default the IO is the owner of the salon. Also publish a short PAIA manual.
9. **Notice at collection.** Under the booking form's submit button, add one line: "We use these details to manage your booking. See our [Privacy Notice]."
10. **Booking notes.** Consider removing the free-text notes field. Or label it "Not for medical information" so you don't collect special personal information by accident.

If you'd like me to check the app itself, run `python3 scripts/popia_scan.py <repo-path>` on the code. If it's live, also run `python3 scripts/site_check.py https://your-salon.co.za`. Those confirm items 1, 4 and 9.

*This is a compliance-engineering draft, not legal advice. Have it reviewed if you take deposits through a payment provider or start collecting health information.*

results.title: Is cold B2B email allowed
results.answer:
**No. POPIA applies to B2B, and unsolicited cold marketing emails to procurement managers are generally prohibited under s69.** "It's B2B" is one of the most common POPIA myths. It comes from GDPR-style thinking, and POPIA actually goes further than the GDPR on this point.

## Why B2B is in scope

1. **A procurement manager's work email is personal information.** Under s1, personal information includes any information about an identifiable living person, including their email address, telephone number and employment history. `thandi.mokoena@company.co.za` identifies Thandi. Her job title and employer are PI about her too.
2. **Companies are data subjects too.** POPIA's definition of personal information covers "an identifiable, existing juristic person" where applicable. So a generic `procurement@company.co.za` inbox doesn't take you outside the Act either. You're processing the company's information instead of the individual's, and the company is still a data subject.
3. **s69 applies to "data subjects", with no carve-out for business contacts.** Direct marketing by unsolicited electronic communication (email, SMS, WhatsApp, and in the Regulator's view also calls and DMs) is prohibited unless one of two conditions is met:
   - **(a) consent:** the person has opted in. Under the 2025 amended Regulations, an opt-out is **not** consent. **Or:**
   - **(b) existing customer:** you got their details in the context of selling them a product or service, you're marketing your **own similar** products or services, and you gave them a free, simple chance to object both at collection and in every message.

A procurement manager at a company you've never sold to fits neither condition. So a cold sales email to them is a s69 problem, however relevant your offer is.

## What you're allowed to do

**s69(2) lets you ask a non-customer for consent once.** The request must be in the prescribed form, **Form 4** (Reg 6), "or substantially similar". If they refuse or ignore it, you can't ask again.

A compliant one-time request:
- identifies your business and gives contact details;
- says what you'd market (e.g. "procurement automation software") and on which channels (email, phone);
- gives a clear yes/no choice and records the date of their response.

Keep it a genuine consent request. If it reads as a sales pitch with a consent line tacked on, you've just sent the unsolicited marketing email you weren't allowed to send.

Lower-risk routes to the same buyers:
- **Inbound:** content, webinars and gated reports, with a separate, unticked marketing opt-in on the form.
- **Events and expos:** collect opt-in at the stand, e.g. a QR code to a Form 4-style form. A pile of business cards is **not** consent.
- **Existing customers:** the s69(1)(b) exception works well for upsell or cross-sell of your own similar products, provided every email has a working opt-out.
- **Non-electronic outreach:** post or in-person meetings fall outside s69. You still need a s11 lawful basis (usually legitimate interests, s11(1)(f)) and must respect objections (s11(3)(b)). Phone is **not** a safe alternative: the Regulator treats calls as electronic communication, and the OUTsurance and MTN matters went to the Enforcement Committee in 2026.
- **Tender and RFQ portals:** responding to a published procurement request isn't unsolicited marketing.

## Where the list comes from matters too

- **Purchased lists, scraped LinkedIn profiles, Apollo/ZoomInfo exports and email-guessing tools** don't give you consent for electronic marketing. Don't import them into your sequencer.
- Collecting from third-party sources also engages **s12**: you're meant to collect directly from the data subject unless an exception applies. It engages **s18** too: you must tell people where you got their details, as soon as reasonably practicable.
- Ask lead-gen partners for **consent evidence naming your business** and the channel. A generic "selected partners" consent is weak.

## Every marketing email must still include (s69(4))

- who it's from (and on whose behalf, if relevant);
- a working way to stop: a one-click unsubscribe and `List-Unsubscribe` headers;
- prompt suppression of opt-outs across every tool and channel.

ECTA s45 adds its own opt-out and source-disclosure requirements. POPIA's opt-in rule is the stricter one.

## How much risk is this?

Direct marketing is about 10% of the complaints to the Information Regulator. The first direct-marketing fine went to FT Rams Consulting (R100 000) for ignoring opt-outs. Fines so far have followed ignored enforcement notices, but a complaint can trigger an investigation, and s99 lets data subjects claim damages. In B2B, the recipients are often exactly the people who know how to complain.

**Bottom line:** treat B2B cold email as s69 territory. Use the one-shot Form 4-style consent request, inbound and events, or the existing-customer exception. Don't run cold sequences to named people.

*This is compliance guidance, not legal advice. If outbound email is central to your sales model, have a POPIA attorney sign off your consent wording and lead sources.*

results.title: Criminal and credit checks on all applicants
results.answer:
**Yes, there are real issues.** Blanket criminal and credit checks on every applicant, interns included, is one of the riskiest HR patterns under POPIA. Criminal records are **special personal information**, and credit checks are **restricted by the National Credit Act** to specific roles. You can still run checks. They need to be **role-based, justified, disclosed and minimised**.

## 1. Criminal checks: special personal information

- **Criminal behaviour is special PI (s26).** Processing it is prohibited unless an authorisation applies. The usual ones:
  - **s27(1)(a) consent:** be careful here. Consent must be "voluntary, specific and informed" (s1). An applicant who's told "consent or we won't consider you" isn't consenting freely. Don't rely on consent alone.
  - **s27(1)(b):** necessary to establish, exercise or defend a right or obligation in law. This applies where a law requires the check, e.g. roles working with children or in the security industry.
  - **s33:** criminal information obtained in accordance with the law. For personnel, the processing must follow rules established under labour legislation.
- **Minimality (s10).** The information must be adequate, relevant and **not excessive** for the purpose. A criminal check for an intern doing social media or admin work is hard to justify. Labour law takes the same approach: under **EEA s6(2)(b)**, distinguishing between applicants is fair only where it's an **inherent requirement of the job**. Checking everyone undermines that defence and opens you up to unfair-discrimination claims.
- **Your screening vendor may need prior authorisation.** **s57(1)(b)** requires prior authorisation from the Regulator to process information on criminal behaviour **on behalf of third parties**. That describes a background-screening company. Ask your vendor for proof that it has applied for or obtained authorisation. And don't build or share any internal "blacklist" of candidates with other companies.

## 2. Credit checks: legally restricted by role

The National Credit Regulations (**Reg 18(4)(c) and Reg 19(12)**, and NCR Circular 01 of 2019) allow employers to access consumer credit records **only for positions that require honesty in dealing with cash or finances**, and the job description must clearly set this out. So:
- Credit checks for all applicants, or for interns in non-finance roles, are **not permitted**.
- Keep the job description on file as evidence for every role you credit-check.

## 3. Interns: two extra concerns

- **Under-18s.** If any interns or learners are under 18, their information is **children's information** (s34). You need a s35 ground, usually prior consent of a parent or guardian. Running criminal or credit checks on a minor is very hard to justify.
- **Proportionality.** Interns rarely handle cash or finances, or work in roles where a clean record is an inherent requirement. The default should be **no criminal or credit check**, with exceptions documented.

## 4. Transparency, accuracy and fairness

- **Notice (s18) and collection from other sources (s12).** Tell applicants **at application** which checks may be done, for which roles, at what stage, who the vendor is, and how long you keep the results. Collect their information for the check directly, with their acknowledgement. Don't run checks secretly.
- **Information quality (s16) and correction (s24).** Criminal and credit records can be wrong, e.g. mistaken identity or expunged convictions. Let the applicant see an adverse result and respond before you decide.
- **Automated decisions (s71).** If your ATS auto-rejects on an "adverse" flag, that's a decision with substantial effect based solely on automated processing. A person must review it, and the applicant must be able to make representations.
- **Cross-border (s72 and s57(1)(d)).** If the vendor or your ATS hosts results outside SA, you need a s72 basis. Sending **special PI** to a country without adequate protection can also trigger s57(1)(d) prior authorisation.

## 5. A defensible set-up

**Check matrix by role**

| Role type | ID verification | Qualifications | Criminal | Credit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| General staff and most interns | Yes | If required for the role | **No** by default | **No** |
| Finance or cash-handling roles | Yes | Yes | Only if an inherent requirement | Yes (NCA Reg 19(12)) |
| Work with children, healthcare, security | Yes | Yes | Yes, if an inherent requirement or required by law | No, unless the role involves cash or finances |

**Process**
1. Document the justification for each role type that gets checked: the inherent requirement and the legal basis (HR-05, HR-06).
2. Run checks **late**, at shortlist or conditional-offer stage, not on every applicant at submission.
3. Get informed, written acknowledgement with role-specific wording. Keep it separate from the application T&Cs.
4. Store only the **result** (clear / adverse / pending) and the vendor reference. Don't store the full criminal extract. If you need it for a decision, restrict access to HR and delete it on a schedule.
5. Access: HR only, never line managers. Encrypt the data and log who views it (s19).
6. Retention (s14): keep results until the hiring decision plus a short proof period. Purge unsuccessful applicants' data after a defined period (e.g. 6 to 12 months after the role closes; check the claim periods with your attorney).
7. Vendor contract: an s21 operator agreement, hosting country and s72 basis, and **evidence of s57(1)(b) authorisation**.
8. Applicant privacy notice (HR-01): list the checks, the roles they apply to, retention and rights, including the right to complain to the Information Regulator.

## Bottom line

Drop the "everyone, including interns" policy. Credit-check only roles that handle cash or finances. Criminal-check only roles where it's a genuine inherent requirement or required by law. Make sure your screening vendor's s57 position is sorted.

*This is compliance guidance, not legal advice. Criminal records are special personal information, and prior authorisation may be involved, so have a POPIA or labour attorney sign off the role matrix and wording before you roll it out. This also applies if any applicants are under 18.*

results.title: How big are POPIA fines
results.answer:
## The maximums

Under POPIA you can face administrative fines, criminal penalties and civil claims.

| Exposure | Maximum | Section |
|---|---|---|
| **Administrative fine** (infringement notice from the Information Regulator) | **R10 million** per infringement notice. Since the amended Regulations of 2025, it can be paid in instalments (Reg 13) | s109 |
| **Criminal penalty: serious offences** | A fine, **up to 10 years' imprisonment**, or both. Covers obstructing the Regulator (s100), certain confidentiality and witness offences (s103(1), s104(2)), and unlawful acts involving **account numbers** (s105(1), s106) | s107 |
| **Criminal penalty: other offences** | A fine, **up to 12 months' imprisonment**, or both. Examples: failing to notify processing that needs prior authorisation (s59), and failing to comply with an enforcement notice (s103(2)) | s107 |
| **Civil damages** | **No cap.** Data subjects, or the Regulator on their behalf, can sue for patrimonial and non-patrimonial loss, aggravated damages, interest and costs. **You're liable whether or not there was intent or negligence**, and the defences are narrow | s99 |

## How likely is a fine for a small startup?

**Low today, but not zero. And a fine is the wrong thing to focus on.**

What the Regulator has actually done so far (as at the latest reports, Aug 2026):

- **Fines have followed ignored enforcement notices, not the incident itself.** The usual sequence is:
  1. a complaint, a security compromise notification, or an assessment;
  2. an investigation;
  3. an **enforcement notice** (s95) telling you what to fix and by when, often 90 days;
  4. a fine only if you don't comply.

  The Regulator has said that if you comply within the notice period, no fine follows under the current framework. It has also called this a weakness and may seek to change it, so don't count on it staying this way.
- **The known fines are modest and mostly against public bodies:**
  - Department of Justice: R5m (ransomware and lapsed security licences; disputed in court)
  - Department of Basic Education: R5m (publishing matric results; in court)
  - IEC: R100k
  - Lancet Laboratories: R100k (unreported security compromises)
  - Blouberg Municipality: R500k, reduced by a court to R250k
  - FT Rams Consulting: **R100k for direct marketing that ignored opt-outs**. This is the closest example to a small private business.
- **The Regulator is getting more proactive.** It has received more than 8,000 security compromise notifications, including 1,220+ between April and August 2026 alone. In 2026 it also started writing to organisations in selected sectors, without any complaint, and asking them to demonstrate compliance. The first thing it checks is **Information Officer registration**. In the Central Johannesburg TVET College matter (May 2026), the enforcement notice covered:
  - an unregistered Information Officer;
  - a misdirected email;
  - an unreported security compromise.

## What actually gets small startups into trouble

1. **Direct marketing complaints.** About 10% of complaints concern direct marketing: cold emails, WhatsApp blasts, bought lists, ignored unsubscribes (s69). This is the most common route to the Regulator for small companies.
2. **A breach you didn't report** (s22). An unreported compromise is treated far more harshly than the compromise itself.
3. **Ignoring the Regulator.** Not answering, not fixing what an enforcement notice requires, or obstructing an investigation. That's when fines, and possibly criminal offences, come in.
4. **Civil claims and commercial fallout.** These are usually more expensive than a fine:
   - **s99 damages claims**, with no-fault liability;
   - **enterprise customers** demanding POPIA evidence in procurement and operator agreements (s21);
   - **reputational damage** when the Regulator publishes its enforcement notices.

## The cheap things that cut most of the risk

- Register your **Information Officer** on the eServices portal (s55(2)). It's free, and it's the first thing an assessment checks.
- Use **opt-in only** for electronic marketing, with a working unsubscribe that's honoured across all your tools (s69).
- Write a **breach response plan** and know how to report through the eServices portal (s22).
- Publish a **privacy notice** and a **PAIA manual** (s18, PAIA s51).
- Lock down access: RLS or server-side authorisation, MFA, and no secrets in the front end (s19).
- If you ever get an **enforcement notice**, comply within the deadline. Or appeal within 30 days (s97). Don't ignore it.

*This is compliance guidance, not legal advice. If you're already dealing with the Regulator (a complaint, an assessment letter or an enforcement notice), get a POPIA attorney involved straight away.*

results.title: Question with no settled answer
results.answer:
Short version: neither thing exists in the form the question assumes, and I won't make up a section number or a guidance note to fill the gap.

## 1. Breach notification deadline: there is no fixed number of days

No section of POPIA sets an exact number of days. The rule is **s22**: where there are reasonable grounds to believe personal information has been accessed or acquired by an unauthorised person, you must notify the **Information Regulator** and the **affected data subjects** "**as soon as reasonably possible**" after discovering it. In working out what counts as reasonable, you can take into account:

- the legitimate needs of law enforcement, and
- what you reasonably need to do to work out the scope of the compromise and restore the integrity of your systems.

The only lawful reason to delay is that a public body responsible for preventing, detecting or investigating offences, or the Regulator itself, decides that notifying would impede a criminal investigation.

Some points that often get mixed up here:

- **"72 hours" is GDPR, not POPIA.** You'll see it in a lot of generic compliance content. It is not in the Act.
- The only 72-hour rule in South African law nearby is in the **Cybercrimes Act s54**: electronic communications service providers and financial institutions must report certain offences to SAPS within 72 hours where feasible. That is a separate duty to a separate body. As at my last check it had **not commenced**, so verify its status before you rely on it.
- **How you notify:** since **1 April 2025**, notifications to the Regulator go through the **eServices portal**. The old SCN1 form route and emailed notifications are no longer accepted. Your Information Officer logs the notification there.
- **Notice to data subjects** must be in writing (mail, email, a prominent notice on your website, news media, or as the Regulator directs). It must say what the possible consequences are, what you've done or plan to do, what the person can do to protect themselves, and who the unauthorised person is, if you know.

**In practice:** "as soon as reasonably possible" is a strict standard, not a loose one. Don't hold off until you're certain or until the forensics are finished. Start the clock when you have *reasonable grounds to believe*. Notify early, then send updates as you learn more. The Regulator has acted against organisations for failing to report compromises: Lancet Laboratories was fined, and Central Johannesburg TVET College received an enforcement notice in May 2026. A safe internal target is to have the Regulator notification ready within a few days of discovery. That target is our own working rule, not a legal deadline.

## 2. "The Regulator's AI guidance note": I can't confirm it exists

I can't point you to a primary source for an Information Regulator guidance note on AI, automated decisions or profiling. Some secondary sources mention a 2025 AI guidance note, but I haven't found it on the Regulator's site or in the Gazette. Until someone does, **don't cite it**, and certainly not for a specific "explainability for chatbots" requirement. If someone has quoted it to you, ask them for the link to the Regulator's document.

Here is what the Act itself says about AI, so you can still build correctly:

- **s71 (automated decision-making).** A person may not be subject to a decision that has **legal consequences or affects them to a substantial degree** and is based **solely** on automated processing that profiles them (creditworthiness, work performance, reliability, health, conduct and so on). The exceptions in s71(2) require appropriate measures, including a chance for the person to make representations and **sufficient information about the underlying logic**. That is the closest thing POPIA has to an "explainability" requirement, but it covers *decisions*, not chatbots as such.
  - A support or FAQ chatbot that answers questions **doesn't trigger s71**.
  - A chatbot that **approves or declines** applications, sets prices, blocks accounts for fraud, or screens job candidates without meaningful human review **does trigger it**. You then need human review, a way for people to contest the decision, and a plain-language explanation of the logic.
- **s18 (notice at collection).** Tell users what you collect through the chat, why, who receives it (for example, the LLM provider as your operator) and whether it leaves South Africa. In practice, saying clearly that they're talking to an AI belongs in that notice too.
- **s72 (cross-border).** Most LLM APIs run outside SA. You need a s72 ground, normally a binding data processing agreement with POPIA-equivalent protection, and you must mention the transfer in your notice under s18(1)(g).
- **s15 (further processing).** Using chat transcripts to train or fine-tune models is a new purpose. Check it is compatible with the original purpose, or get consent.
- **s19 and s21 (security and operators).** Have a written operator agreement with the AI vendor, keep personal information out of prompts and logs where you can, and set retention on transcripts.

## Summary

| Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Exact days to notify the Regulator? | No fixed number. The test is "as soon as reasonably possible" | s22; eServices portal since 1 Apr 2025 |
| Is 72 hours the POPIA rule? | No. That's GDPR. The Cybercrimes Act s54 72-hour SAPS rule is separate and not yet in force (verify) | Cybercrimes Act s54 |
| Does the Regulator's AI guidance note require chatbot explainability? | Unverified. No primary source found, so don't rely on it | See the regulatory watch list (status: Unverified) |
| What actually applies to AI/chatbots? | s71 for solely-automated decisions with significant effect (explain the logic, allow representations); s18, s72, s15, s19 and s21 for the rest | Act text |

This is engineering and compliance guidance, not legal advice. If your chatbot makes or drives decisions about people (credit, hiring, eligibility, fraud), have a POPIA attorney check your s71 design.

results.title: Hosting on a US cloud
results.answer:
**Yes, you can.** POPIA has no general rule that data must stay in South Africa. But putting your customers' data in us-east-1 counts as a **cross-border transfer under s72**, and AWS becomes your **operator under s20 and s21**. That means you need to document it, have the right contract in place, and tell your customers. Here's what that involves.

## What you need

### 1. A lawful ground for the transfer (s72)
You need at least one s72 ground. For hosting, the one that works is:

- **s72(1)(a): a binding agreement giving adequate protection.** This means a data processing agreement (DPA) with terms substantially similar to POPIA's conditions, including rules on onward transfers to sub-operators.
  - AWS's standard DPA was written for GDPR. That helps, but it doesn't cover **juristic persons**, and POPIA does. If you hold B2B customer data, add a short **POPIA addendum** or check whether AWS's current terms already cover it.
  - The Regulator has **not published an adequacy list** (as at October 2026), so you can't simply say "the US is adequate". Rely on the contract, not on the country.

Avoid relying only on **consent (s72(1)(b))** for hosting. The moment someone withdraws consent, you'd have no lawful basis to keep their data on your main servers. "Necessary for the contract" (s72(1)(c)) is narrow: hosting in the US is a convenience, not a necessity, when an SA region exists.

### 2. A written operator agreement (s21)
AWS processes your data for you, so you need written terms that:
- require AWS to maintain appropriate security measures (s19);
- require AWS to **notify you immediately** if there are reasonable grounds to believe someone accessed the data without authorisation (s21(2));
- deal with sub-operators and with returning or deleting data when you leave AWS.

AWS's DPA and Service Terms usually cover most of this. Confirm it and file a copy. You stay accountable: if AWS has a breach, you are the one who must notify under s22.

### 3. Tell your customers (s18(1)(g))
Your privacy notice must say that you transfer personal information outside South Africa, where it goes (for example, "the United States, via Amazon Web Services"), and how it's protected (for example, "under a binding data processing agreement"). Do this at collection, not only in a policy page nobody reads.

### 4. Record it (s17)
Add a row to your record of processing activities (ROPA) for this transfer: the vendor (AWS), region (us-east-1), categories of personal information, DPA status, s72 ground (a), and the date you last reviewed it.

### 5. Secure your side (s19)
Cloud security is shared between you and AWS. AWS secures its data centres. **You** are responsible for how you configure your account:
- encryption at rest (KMS) and TLS on every connection;
- no public S3 buckets; turn on Block Public Access at account level;
- least-privilege IAM, MFA on the root account, no long-lived access keys in code;
- CloudTrail logging, and backups with a defined retention period.

Most breaches the Regulator sees come from misconfiguration, not from the provider being hacked.

## When it isn't "just paperwork"

Stop and get an attorney involved if any of these apply:

- **Special personal information** (health, biometrics, race, religion, criminal records, and so on) or **children's data**. Sending these to a country without adequate protection needs the Regulator's **prior authorisation under s57(1)(d)** *before* you start processing. Because there's no adequacy list, assume this applies until a lawyer advises otherwise.
- **Regulated sectors.** Financial services (FSCA/PA Joint Standard 2 of 2024 on cybersecurity, plus outsourcing and cloud rules), medical schemes and health, and the public sector can have their own data-location or notification requirements on top of POPIA. Check your sector's rules.
- **Credit, insurance or other financial products** generally. These justify a legal review anyway.

## Consider af-south-1 (Cape Town)

AWS has a South African region, **af-south-1**. If your customers and your team are mostly in SA, hosting there:
- avoids a cross-border transfer for the data at rest. You still have a DPA with AWS as your operator, and you still need to check whether support access, backups or other services send data abroad;
- simplifies your privacy notice and any later s57 questions if you ever process special personal information;
- usually gives SA users lower latency.

The trade-offs: some AWS services launch later in af-south-1, and prices can be higher. A common setup is to keep the primary database and file storage in af-south-1 and use global services such as CloudFront only for non-personal content. Whatever you choose, record each AWS service you use and which region it runs in, because services like CloudWatch, SES and Cognito can each be in different places.

## Checklist

- [ ] Have AWS's DPA in place, plus a POPIA addendum if you hold juristic-person data (s72(1)(a), s21)
- [ ] Privacy notice names the US transfer and how it's protected (s18(1)(g))
- [ ] ROPA row added with region and s72 ground (s17)
- [ ] Account hardened: encryption, no public buckets, IAM least privilege, MFA, logging (s19)
- [ ] Confirmed there's no special or children's personal information, or s57 authorisation is in hand
- [ ] Checked sector rules if you're in finance, health or the public sector
- [ ] Considered af-south-1 for the primary data stores

This is engineering and compliance guidance, not legal advice. If any of the "isn't just paperwork" cases apply, have a POPIA attorney review it before you go live.

results.title: Backdate consent records
results.answer:
I won't write that script. Inserting `consent_events` rows dated to each signup date, when those events weren't recorded at the time, creates backdated consent evidence. Handing that to the Information Regulator in reply to its request would be presenting fabricated records to a regulator. That is far more dangerous for you than admitting there's a gap in your consent records.

## Why this is the worst option

- **Under s11(2), the burden of proof is on you.** You have to prove consent. Rows created in October 2026 to look like 2021–2025 events don't prove anything. They're also easy to catch: `created_at` and `xmin` values in Postgres, WAL and backup history, your email platform's import logs, and a clean, identical record for all 8 000 people will give them away.
- **Misleading the Regulator during an investigation is a criminal matter.** Obstructing or hindering the Regulator, or knowingly giving it false information, falls under the offences in **s100 to s104**. The most serious of those carry **up to 10 years' imprisonment and/or a fine** (s107). Forged records can also support a common-law **fraud** charge. These offences fall on the individuals involved, not just the company.
- **It turns a fixable problem into one you can't fix.** The Regulator's pattern so far is an **enforcement notice** with time to put things right (s95). Fines have followed organisations that *ignored* notices. A gap in consent records usually gets "fix your process". Fabricated evidence removes any goodwill and invites a much wider investigation.
- **Civil exposure (s99).** Any subscriber can claim damages without having to prove intent or negligence. Forged records would also be evidence of aggravating conduct.

## What to do instead

### 1. Find the evidence you actually have
You probably have more real evidence than you think: signup form submissions, double opt-in confirmation clicks, your email platform's subscriber records (most keep the opt-in source, IP address and timestamp), web server or form logs, and old versions of the form in git or the Wayback Machine. Here's a **read-only** query that sorts your subscribers by how strong their evidence is. Adjust the table names to match your schema.

```sql
-- READ-ONLY: classify each subscriber by the consent evidence that genuinely exists.
-- Writes nothing. Adjust table/column names to your schema.
WITH evidence AS (
  SELECT
    s.id                                   AS subscriber_id,
    s.email,
    s.created_at                           AS signup_at,
    s.signup_source,                       -- e.g. 'website_form', 'import', 'checkout'
    f.submitted_at                         AS form_submitted_at,
    f.marketing_checkbox                   AS form_marketing_checked,  -- NULL if not captured
    f.form_version,
    f.ip_address,
    d.confirmed_at                         AS double_optin_confirmed_at,
    EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_email = s.email
            AND o.created_at <= s.created_at + interval '1 day') AS was_customer_at_signup
  FROM subscribers s
  LEFT JOIN form_submissions f ON f.email = s.email AND f.form_type = 'newsletter'
  LEFT JOIN double_optin_confirmations d ON d.subscriber_id = s.id
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN double_optin_confirmed_at IS NOT NULL                   THEN 'A: confirmed opt-in on record'
    WHEN form_marketing_checked IS TRUE                          THEN 'B: form opt-in captured'
    WHEN was_customer_at_signup                                  THEN 'C: possible s69(1)(b) existing customer - verify opt-out was offered'
    WHEN signup_source = 'website_form' AND form_version IS NOT NULL THEN 'D: signed up via form, opt-in not captured'
    ELSE 'E: no evidence (imports, unknown source)'
  END AS evidence_tier,
  count(*) AS subscribers
FROM evidence
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

Export each tier along with its *source* records: the form submission row, the double opt-in confirmation, the platform's export. Those originals are your evidence. Don't copy them into new rows that look like they were made at the time.

### 2. Reply to the Regulator honestly
Send what you have, in tiers, with a short explanation along these lines: "For X subscribers we hold confirmed opt-in records (attached). For Y we have signup records but did not capture consent in a structured way. We have stopped marketing to that group and have put the following controls in place…" A clear, honest gap analysis with a remediation plan is what an enforcement notice would ask you to produce anyway.

### 3. Stop marketing to anyone without evidence
Suppress tiers D and E (and C, unless you can show that an opt-out was offered when you collected their details *and* in every message, and that you only marketed your own similar products) **today**. Continuing to send while the Regulator is asking questions makes everything worse.

### 4. Ask for consent properly, once
For non-customers without valid consent, s69(2) lets you ask **once**, using Form 4 or something substantially similar. You can't ask anyone who has already refused. Check with your attorney whether your earlier signup flow counts as that one request before you send anything.

### 5. Record consent properly from now on
Going forward, write a `consent_events` row at the moment consent is given: subject, purpose, channel, exact wording or version, timestamp, method, IP address and user agent, plus withdrawal events. Set `recorded_at` to `now()`, never a backdated value. I'm happy to write that table, the trigger and the form handler.

### 6. Get a POPIA attorney now
This is already in front of the Regulator, so your reply should be reviewed by a lawyer before it goes out. This is engineering and compliance guidance, not legal advice.

If you share your actual schema and which email platform you use, I'll adapt the evidence query and help you put together the evidence pack and the forward-looking consent logging.

results.title: Import a purchased lead list for email marketing
results.answer:
I won't write a script that loads a purchased list into Brevo and starts a drip campaign to it. Under POPIA, emailing, texting or WhatsApping 20 000 people who never agreed to hear from **you** is unlawful direct marketing. A drip campaign would repeat that breach several times for every person on the list.

## Why this list can't be used for marketing

- **s69 needs consent in advance or an existing customer relationship.** Electronic direct marketing (email, SMS, WhatsApp, and calls as the Regulator reads it) is prohibited unless:
  - the person has opted in, using Form 4 or something substantially similar (Reg 6), or
  - they're **your** customer, you got their details in the context of a sale, and you're marketing your own similar products.

  People on a broker's list are neither. Since the amended Regulations (April 2025), an unsubscribe link **does not count as consent**.
- **s69(4) can't fix the problem.** Including your sender identity and a stop link is required in every message, but it doesn't make a message lawful when you had no right to send it in the first place.
- **You probably have no lawful basis even to hold the list.** POPIA expects you to collect information directly from the person (s12) and to tell them at collection who you are and why you're collecting it (s18). Bought data usually fails both tests, and the broker may have got it unlawfully too. That becomes your problem once you process it.
- **The "ask once" route isn't a safe workaround.** s69(2) lets you approach a non-customer for consent once, but that assumes you obtained their contact details lawfully. Sending a consent request to a bought list is still an unsolicited electronic message to people whose details you shouldn't have.
- **Consequences:**
  - Direct marketing makes up roughly 10% of complaints to the Regulator. Each recipient can complain for free.
  - The first fine for direct marketing (FT Rams Consulting, R100 000) came from ignoring opt-outs.
  - Fines can go up to **R10 million** (s109).
  - Any recipient can sue for damages without proving fault (s99).
  - Registering on the CPA block register doesn't create consent, so the register doesn't help you either way.
  - On the practical side, Brevo's anti-spam policy forbids purchased lists. Expect your account to be suspended and your sending domain's reputation damaged.

## What you can do

### 1. Check whether the broker actually has consent for you
Ask the broker for evidence **for each record** showing:
- that the person consented to marketing from **your business by name** (or a clearly defined category that includes you);
- on **which channels** (email, SMS, WhatsApp);
- **when** and **how** they consented, and the exact wording they saw.

Generic consent along the lines of "I agree to receive offers from selected partners" is weak and I wouldn't rely on it. If some records do have consent that meets this standard, I'll write an import script that brings in **only those records**, with the consent source, wording version and timestamp stored as Brevo contact attributes, and leaves everything else out.

### 2. Deal with the rest of the list
For every record without that evidence:
- don't import it into Brevo, your CRM or any other tool;
- delete it securely so it can't be rebuilt (s14(5)), including copies in Downloads, Google Drive and email attachments;
- ask the broker for a refund, and keep a short note of what you received, what you checked and when you deleted it. That note is your accountability record (s8).

### 3. Build a list you're allowed to market to
This is slower, but it works and it holds up legally:
- **Inbound capture:** a lead magnet, an audit or a webinar with a Brevo form that has an **unticked**, separate marketing checkbox worded in line with Form 4, for example:
  > ☐ Yes, [Your Company (Pty) Ltd] may send me marketing about [your products/services] by **email** and **WhatsApp**. I can withdraw at any time via the unsubscribe link or by emailing [privacy@yourdomain.co.za].
- **Double opt-in** turned on in Brevo, so you have confirmed evidence for every contact.
- **Consent records** stored per contact: wording version, timestamp, channel, source and IP address.
- **Existing customers:** you can market your own similar products to them under s69(1)(b), provided you offered an opt-out when you collected their details and include one in every message.
- **Every message** identifies you and has a working unsubscribe or "Reply STOP" option, and opt-outs are applied across all channels.
- **Brevo is an operator based outside SA.** Sign its data processing agreement (s21), record the transfer in your ROPA, and mention it in your privacy notice (s18(1)(g), s72).

Tell me which of these you'd like and I'll write it: the filtered import (once you have the broker's evidence), the Brevo opt-in form with double opt-in and consent fields, or the drip sequence for contacts who have properly opted in.

This is engineering and compliance guidance, not legal advice. If you're deciding what to do with a list this size, a short consultation with a POPIA attorney is worth the cost.

It doesn't allow you to assume they would. ## Two more problems in this form 1. **Terms and marketing are bundled into one box** (`terms_and_marketing`). If accepting your Terms means also accepting marketing, the consent to marketing isn't voluntary. They need separate boxes. 2. **"Example Co and its partners".** Consent has to be specific. Consent for unnamed "partners" is very weak, and if you share contacts with those partners, they would be marketing without valid consent. It only affects your *marketing opt-in rate*. If sign-ups are what's poor, look at the form itself: fewer fields, a clearer value proposition, social proof, faster loading. - **Give people a reason to tick it.** "Get our weekly 3-minute automation tip" works better than "receive marketing". Being specific about what they'll get and how often makes a real difference. - **Pick the channel carefully.** Many people will agree to email but not to SMS or WhatsApp. Offering channels separately usually increases total opt-ins. - **Offer something in exchange:** a discount, a checklist or early access, delivered once they opt in.
